prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision measurement

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks combine a clean, original idea (Katori's magic-wavelength trapping, which removes the lattice light shift) with a decisive experimental realisation (the first strontium lattice clock, then Ye's record accuracy and stability at the 1e-18 level and the many-body clock work). Performance has been reproduced and compared across several national and university laboratories, so the result is robust rather than a single-group claim. It makes a new regime measurable: tests of constants, relativistic redshift across millimetre scales, dark-matter searches, and a credible basis for redefining the second. Five of eight openings put it in the top three, including mine at rank 2, and the two-name credit is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist. I ranked circuit QED first in my opening, but after reading the ballots I think the clock case is the stronger one to put forward. It has broad support from colleagues who read it independently, and it avoids my own proximity problem and the recency problem of the 2025 circuit prize.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision frequency metrology has been recognised repeatedly (Hall and Haensch for combs in 2005, Wineland and Haroche in 2012), and Ye already shares the 2005 prize. A critic can say the lattice clock is an extraordinary refinement of an already-honoured chain rather than a new discovery. The SI second has not yet been redefined, and contributors such as Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Hinkley sit outside a two-name credit. The strongest answer is that the magic-wavelength idea changed how many atoms can be interrogated at once, which is what made the 1e-18 regime and many-body clock physics reachable. That is a conceptual step, not only an engineering gain, but the committee must be able to state it clearly in the citation.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first as an instrument that changes what can be measured, and ranks circuit QED second with a proposed split of Schoelkopf, Wallraff and Girvin, noting that the 2025 prize touches the same community.
responses.response: I agree on the clock and on the timing concern for circuit QED, and I now weigh that concern more heavily than in my opening. I do not agree that Girvin should take the theory slot in place of Blais. The 2004 proposal was a joint paper, and Blais did the central dispersive-regime and readout analysis, so the theory attribution is genuinely unsettled. That is one more reason I would hold circuit QED back for a later year, when the 2025 prize has had time to settle and the attribution can be argued without rushing.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that lattice clocks are a clean two-laureate case, that the 2005 and 2012 prizes cover neighbouring ground but not this invention, and that confirmation across JILA, RIKEN, PTB, SYRTE and others is strong and timely.
responses.response: I largely agree, but the novelty point needs sharper wording than 'neighbouring ground'. Ye's 2005 share was for combs, and the committee will be asked whether this is a second prize for the same programme. I would answer that the lattice clock is a different physical idea: many atoms confined at the magic wavelength, with Doppler and recoil effects suppressed, where the earlier recognised work used single ions or the frequency comb as a readout tool. The citation should therefore name the magic-wavelength lattice concept explicitly. I would also like us to record why Lemonde and Takamoto are not included, since the priority history is partly from memory and none of us has checked it against the primary papers.

responses.point: Olsson ranks the topological insulator candidate first, as an original prediction followed by a decisive HgTe edge-conductance experiment, and ranks the lattice clock second while asking whether the prize should wait for the SI second redefinition.
responses.response: I ranked B038 last in my own list because I am outside condensed matter, so I defer to you on its standing. I would still push back on the idea of waiting for the redefinition. The prize is for the invention and its verified performance, which do not depend on a metrology committee's timetable, and the redefinition will not change the science. My concern with the topological insulator is attribution. The HgTe quantum-well proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is the specific prediction Molenkamp's group tested, and it is not in the credited trio. Zhang's death simplifies the names but does not make it less of a hole. If the condensed-matter colleagues can show that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is a defensible account of the discovery, I would take it seriously as the strongest competing candidate.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first and quantum key distribution second, proposing Bennett and Brassard alone for BB84 and arguing that Ekert's E91 blurs the priority.
responses.response: On QKD I disagree with leaving Ekert out. E91 is a different protocol whose security rests on Bell inequality violation, and that links it to the 2022 entanglement prize. It is not a variant of BB84. I still rank QKD behind the clock. The principle is clear but the real-device security story is not settled, and Wiesner's prior conjugate-coding idea is a priority caveat we cannot award around. On IceCube, I am outside the field and take your point that the flux is firmly established. A one-name prize for a collaboration of that size troubles me, and I would want to see how the committee would justify leaving out others if Halzen alone were credited.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that the magic-wavelength lattice clock is conceptually distinct from the combs recognised in 2005, given that Ye shares that prize.
Whether Lemonde, Takamoto or Ludlow have a claim strong enough to displace or join Katori and Ye; the priority history is from memory.
Whether a circuit QED prize is better held back until the effect of the 2025 prize on the community has settled, and how to split credit among Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf and Wallraff.
How the topological insulator candidate should handle the omission of Bernevig and Hughes, and its relation to the 2016 topological-phases prize; I cannot judge this from my own field.
statement.conflict_note: Possible recusal issue: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, work closely with superconducting-circuit groups at Chalmers, and have professional proximity to the circuit QED community (B006) and to the 2025 laureates, two of whom visited Chalmers as WACQT guests. I would recuse myself or at least declare the connection on B006, and I would also defer on B033 and B009, where my work overlaps with quantum-information platforms. No specific connection to the optical lattice clock candidates (Katori, Ye) is apparent from my profile.
